claim: Glucagon secretion dysregulation in diabetes fosters hyperglycemia.
source: Glucagon secretion dysregulation in diabetes fosters hyperglycemia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript.

claim: Mice lacking glucagon receptor (Gcgr-/-) do not develop diabetes following streptozotocin (STZ)-mediated ablation of insulin-producing β-cells according to recent studies.
source: Recent studies report that mice lacking glucagon receptor (Gcgr-/-) do not develop diabetes following streptozotocin (STZ)-mediated ablation of insulin-producing β-cells.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings reported in the literature.

claim: Diabetes prevention in STZ-treated Gcgr-/- animals requires remnant insulin action originating from spared residual β-cells.
source: Here, we show that diabetes prevention in STZ-treated Gcgr-/- animals requires remnant insulin action originating from spared residual β-cells
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including insulin receptor blockade experiments.

claim: STZ-treated Gcgr-/- mice became hyperglycemic after insulin receptor blockade.
source: these mice indeed became hyperglycemic after insulin receptor blockade.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A where S961 treatment induced hyperglycemia.

claim: Gcgr-/- mice developed hyperglycemia after induction of a more complete, diphtheria toxin (DT)-induced β-cell loss.
source: Accordingly, Gcgr-/- mice developed hyperglycemia after induction of a more complete, diphtheria toxin (DT)-induced β-cell loss
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating hyperglycemia in DT-treated RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice.

claim: DT-induced β-cell loss represents a situation of near-absolute insulin deficiency similar to type 1 diabetes.
source: a situation of near-absolute insulin deficiency similar to type 1 diabetes.
evidence: This is supported by data showing >99% β-cell loss, very low insulin levels, and diabetes symptoms.

claim: Glucagon deficiency did not impair the natural capacity of α-cells to reprogram into insulin production after extreme β-cell loss.
source: In addition, glucagon deficiency did not impair the natural capacity of α-cells to reprogram into insulin production after extreme β-cell loss.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing bihormonal cells in both Gcgr+/+ and Gcgr-/- mice after DT treatment.

claim: α-to-β-cell conversion was improved in Gcgr-/- mice as a consequence of α-cell hyperplasia.
source: α-to-β-cell conversion was improved in Gcgr-/- mice as a consequence of α-cell hyperplasia.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6C showing increased absolute number of bihormonal cells in Gcgr-/- mice.

claim: Glucagon antagonism could be a useful adjuvant therapy in diabetes only when residual insulin action persists.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that glucagon antagonism could i) be a useful adjuvant therapy in diabetes only when residual insulin action persists
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings throughout the study.

claim: Glucagon antagonism could help devising future β-cell regeneration therapies relying upon α-cell reprogramming.
source: and ii) help devising future β-cell regeneration therapies relying upon α-cell reprogramming.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the finding of increased α-to-β conversion in Gcgr-/- mice.

claim: Glucagon counterbalances the effects of insulin on blood glucose homeostasis by stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
source: Glucagon, a 29-amino acid-long hormone synthetized in pancreatic α-cells through cleavage of its precursor, proglucagon, by prohormone convertase 2 (PC2), counterbalances the effects of insulin on blood glucose homeostasis by stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (Gromada et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior literature.

claim: Insulin and glucagon act in a paracrine fashion to reciprocally regulate α- and β-cell function.
source: In addition, the two hormones act in a paracrine fashion to reciprocally regulate α- and β-cell function (Unger and Orci, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior literature.

claim: Hypersecretion of glucagon in diabetes exacerbates hepatic glucose output, thereby fostering hyperglycemia and ketogenesis.
source: Hypersecretion of glucagon in diabetes exacerbates hepatic glucose output, thereby fostering hyperglycemia and ketogenesis (Unger et al., 1970; Unger, 1971; Sherwin et al., 1976; D'Alessio, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior literature.

claim: Antagonists of glucagon signaling are currently being tested in clinical trials for diabetes.
source: In consequence, antagonists of glucagon signaling are currently being tested in clinical trials for diabetes (Campbell and Drucker, 2015).
evidence: This is cited information about ongoing clinical research.

claim: Gcgr-/- mice and animals lacking α-cells due to pancreatic aristaless-related homeobox (Arx) deficiency did not exhibit the usual signs of diabetes after streptozotocin (STZ)-mediated β-cell destruction.
source: Surprisingly, these animals did not exhibit the usual signs of diabetes, such as hyperglycemia or glucose intolerance, after streptozotocin (STZ)-mediated β-cell destruction (Conarello et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2011; 2012; Hancock et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited information from prior studies.

claim: STZ causes an incomplete β-cell ablation due to variations in administration protocols and in genetic background-dependent sensitivity.
source: Indeed, because STZ causes an incomplete β-cell ablation due to variations in administration protocols and in genetic background-dependent sensitivity (Deeds et al., 2011; Cardinal et al., 1998; Gurley, 2006)
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: The 'diabetes resistance' phenotype of Gcgr-/- mice may rely on the action of insulin from residual β-cells.
source: it is possible that the "diabetes resistance" phenotype of Gcgr-/- mice relies on the action of insulin from residual β-cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on prior observations.

claim: RIP-DTR model leads to an almost complete β-cell elimination.
source: we used a transgenic model of diphtheria toxin (DT)-mediated β-cell ablation, termed RIP-DTR, which leads to an almost complete β-cell elimination (Thorel et al., 2010; Chera et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited information about the RIP-DTR model from prior publications.

claim: Adult RIP-DTR mice spontaneously reconstitute new insulin-producing cells by α-cell transdifferentiation in conditions of severe insulin insufficiency.
source: Also, because adult RIP-DTR mice spontaneously reconstitute new insulin-producing cells by α-cell transdifferentiation in this condition of severe insulin insufficiency
evidence: This is cited information from prior work on the RIP-DTR model.

claim: Compensatory α-cell hyperplasia occurs due to glucagon signaling blockade.
source: we explored whether the compensatory α-cell hyperplasia due to glucagon signaling blockade (Furuta et al., 1997; Gelling et al., 2003; Longuet et al., 2013) influences the reprogramming of α-cells toward insulin production.
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: Near-total β-cell loss triggers severe hyperglycemia and all the metabolic features of type 1 diabetes (cachexia, glucose intolerance, and death) in mice with constitutive or induced glucagon signaling deficiency.
source: Here we show that near-total β-cell loss triggers severe hyperglycemia and all the metabolic features of type 1 diabetes (cachexia, glucose intolerance, and death) in mice with constitutive or induced glucagon signaling deficiency.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The absence of hyperglycemia observed in glucagon-deficient mice after STZ treatment can be explained through the persistence of a residual β-cell mass, which ensures a low level of insulin action.
source: We report that the absence of hyperglycemia observed in glucagon-deficient mice after STZ treatment can be explained through the persistence of a residual β-cell mass, which ensures a low level of insulin action.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by data in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice displayed lower basal glucose levels than controls.
source: RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice, like Gcgr-/- mice, displayed lower basal glucose levels than controls (RIP-DTR;Gcgr+/+ and RIP-DTR;Gcgr+/-; not shown) (Gelling et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with citation to prior work showing similar findings.

claim: Upon DT-induced β-cell ablation, both control and knockout animals developed severe hyperglycemia, with a slower kinetics in RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice.
source: Upon DT-induced β-cell ablation, both control and knockout animals developed severe hyperglycemia, with a slower kinetics in RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RIP-DTR;Gcgr+/- and RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- animals lost weight at similar rates after DT treatment.
source: Animals of both groups lost weight at similar rates (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RIP-DTR;Gcgr+/- and RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- animals died in absence of exogenous insulin treatment after DT-induced β-cell ablation.
source: and died in absence of exogenous insulin treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Administration of long-acting insulin, although insufficient to normalize blood glucose levels, permitted survival and body weight maintenance in DT-treated mice.
source: By contrast, administration of long-acting insulin, although insufficient to normalize blood glucose levels, permitted survival and body weight maintenance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: As soon as insulin treatment was discontinued, blood glucose levels and body weight quickly deteriorated in all groups.
source: As soon as insulin treatment was discontinued, blood glucose levels and body weight quickly deteriorated in all groups.
evidence: This is an observation from the insulin treatment experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gcgr-/- mice are not protected against hyperglycemia after near-total β-cell loss, but develop classical signs of type 1 diabetes and require insulin therapy.
source: Altogether, these findings indicate that Gcgr-/- mice are not protected against hyperglycemia after near-total β-cell loss, but develop classical signs of type 1 diabetes and require insulin therapy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Constitutive Gcgr deletion leads to increased embryonic lethality, and defects in pancreatic development and islet-cell maturation.
source: Constitutive Gcgr deletion leads to increased embryonic lethality, and defects in pancreatic development and islet-cell maturation (Vuguin et al., 2006; Vuguin and Charron, 2011; Ouhilal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: Constitutive Gcgr deletion may encompass long-lasting compensatory metabolic adaptations.
source: Since these abnormalities may encompass long-lasting compensatory metabolic adaptations
evidence: This is an inference based on cited developmental defects.

claim: Anti-GCGR mAb treatment led to a reduction in basal glycemia in C57BL/6 wild type mice.
source: In agreement with a previously described antibody (Gu et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2009), anti-GCGR treatment led to a reduction in basal glycemia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Anti-GCGR treatment triggered α-cell hyperplasia and hypertrophy in wild type mice.
source: and triggered α-cell hyperplasia and hypertrophy, as observed in Gcgr-/- animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D) (Gelling et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Antibody-treated Gcgr+/+ mice showed altered responses to intraperitoneal glucose and insulin tolerance tests, like Gcgr-/- animals.
source: In addition, antibody-treated Gcgr+/+ mice showed altered responses, like Gcgr-/- animals, to intraperitoneal glucose and insulin tolerance tests (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Anti-GCGR administration in Gcgr+/+ mice phenocopies the main metabolic and cellular alterations of Gcgr-/- mice.
source: Anti-GCGR administration in Gcgr+/+ mice therefore phenocopies the main metabolic and cellular alterations of Gcgr-/- mice
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of antibody-treated and Gcgr-/- mice data.

claim: Anti-GCGR mAb represents a valuable tool for inducing glucagon signaling antagonism in vivo.
source: and thus represents a valuable tool for inducing glucagon signaling antagonism in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phenocopy data.

claim: All RIP-DTR mice became severely hyperglycemic and lost weight after DT, regardless of anti-GCGR mAb treatment.
source: In agreement with the above results using RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- animals, all mice became severely hyperglycemic and lost weight after DT, regardless of antibody treatment (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Only insulin administration allowed for survival following β-cell ablation, not glucagon receptor inhibition.
source: Moreover, only insulin administration allowed for survival following β-cell ablation, not glucagon receptor inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lack of glucagon signaling is not sufficient per se to prevent severe hyperglycemia and diabetes following extreme β-cell loss.
source: Collectively, these observations indicate that the lack of glucagon signaling is not sufficient per se to prevent severe hyperglycemia and diabetes following extreme β-cell loss
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DT experiments in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The findings contrast with previous studies in which Gcgr-/-, or anti-GCGR-treated mice did not develop the metabolic manifestations of the disease when β-cell ablation was mediated by STZ.
source: and contrast with previous studies in which Gcgr-/-, or anti-GCGR-treated mice did not develop the metabolic manifestations of the disease when β-cell ablation was mediated by STZ (Conarello et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2011; 2012; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited prior literature.

claim: Nearly 90% of islet sections were totally devoid of β-cells after DT, versus only 45% after STZ in Gcgr-/- mice.
source: Histologically, we observed that nearly 90% of islet sections were totally devoid of β-cells after DT, versus only 45% after STZ (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The β-cell mass was reduced by 98–99% after DT, but only by 70–80% after STZ in Gcgr-/- mice.
source: Accordingly, the β-cell mass and pancreatic insulin content were reduced by 98–99% after DT, but only by 70–80% after STZ (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Plasma insulin levels were just above detection threshold after DT, but readily detectable after STZ in Gcgr-/- mice.
source: In addition, plasma insulin levels were just above detection threshold after DT, but readily detectable after STZ (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by plasma insulin measurement data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: β-cell destruction is more complete after DT- than after STZ-treatment in Gcgr-/- mice.
source: Together, these results indicate that β-cell destruction is more complete after DT- than after STZ-treatment in Gcgr-/- mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative data in Figure 3.

claim: S961 administration in Gcgr+/- mice triggered a strong increase in glycemia.
source: In agreement with its previously reported action, S961 administration in Gcgr+/- mice triggered a strong increase in glycemia (Figure 4A; blue dashed vs black continuous line).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Gcgr-/- animals exhibited a smaller but significant increase in glycemia after S961 treatment, indicating that glucagon deficiency has a beneficial effect in this situation of relative insulin deficit.
source: Interestingly, Gcgr-/- animals exhibited a smaller but significant increase in glycemia, indicating that glucagon deficiency has a beneficial effect in this situation of relative insulin deficit (purple dashed vs red continuous line).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: STZ-treated Gcgr-/- mice remained normoglycemic, as previously reported.
source: Although STZ-treated Gcgr-/- mice remained normoglycemic, as previously reported (Conarello et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2011; 2012)
evidence: This is an observation consistent with cited prior literature.

claim: STZ-treated Gcgr-/- mice developed severe hyperglycemia after insulin receptor inhibition with S961.
source: they developed severe hyperglycemia after insulin receptor inhibition (continuous vs dotted purple line).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Residual insulin action, likely originating from STZ-escaping β-cells, is still present after STZ administration in Gcgr-/- animals, and is necessary to prevent hyperglycemia and diabetes.
source: This suggests that residual insulin action, likely originating from STZ-escaping β-cells, is still present after STZ administration in Gcgr-/- animals, and is necessary to prevent hyperglycemia and diabetes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the S961 experiment data in Figure 4A.

claim: In conditions of glucagon deficiency (Gcgr-/- mice), there was a decreased expression of the gluconeogenic enzyme Pepck and an increased expression of the glycolytic enzyme Gck as compared to Gcgr+/- controls.
source: In conditions of glucagon deficiency (increased insulin/glucagon ratio; Gcgr-/- mice), we observed a decreased expression of the gluconeogenic enzyme Pepck and an increased expression of the glycolytic enzyme Gck as compared to Gcgr+/- controls (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Upon induced insulin deficiency (STZ-, S961-, or DT-treated Gcgr+/- animals), Pepck and Gck exhibited the opposite regulation compared to glucagon deficiency.
source: By contrast, upon induced insulin deficiency (decreased insulin/glucagon ratio), as in STZ-, S961-, or DT-treated Gcgr+/- animals, Pepck and Gck exhibited the opposite regulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DT caused a 1000-fold decrease in Gck expression, suggesting that it led to a more complete suppression of insulin action than STZ or S961.
source: We observed the strongest effect after DT, which caused a 1000-fold decrease in Gck expression, suggesting that it led to a more complete suppression of insulin action than STZ or S961.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RT-qPCR data in Figure 4C.

claim: When inducing insulin insufficiency in a Gcgr-/- background, Pepck and Gck mRNA levels were similar to those measured in untreated Gcgr+/- control mice, except after DT.
source: When inducing insulin insufficiency in a Gcgr-/- background, a situation of combined insulin and glucagon deficiency, we observed Pepck and Gck mRNA levels similar to those measured in untreated Gcgr+/- control mice, except after DT, which induced a strong downregulation of Gck expression in Gcgr-/- livers (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: DT-, but not STZ-treatment depleted liver glycogen stores in RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- animals.
source: Similarly, DT-, but not STZ-treatment depleted liver glycogen stores in RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by glycogen measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lack of glucagon action can compensate for the effect of partial insulin insufficiency on the expression of rate-limiting enzymes and hepatic glycogen metabolism, but not after near-total β-cell loss.
source: These results suggest that lack of glucagon action can compensate for the effect of partial insulin insufficiency on the expression of rate-limiting enzymes and hepatic glycogen metabolism, but not after near-total β-cell loss, a situation where the effect of insulin deficiency outweighs that of glucagon deficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the hepatic gene expression and glycogen data in Figure 4.

claim: FoxO1 mRNA levels were similar in untreated Gcgr+/- and Gcgr-/- mice.
source: FoxO1 mRNA levels were similar in untreated Gcgr+/- and Gcgr-/- mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In Gcgr-/- animals, STZ or S961 administration did not significantly affect FoxO1 expression.
source: In Gcgr-/- animals, STZ or S961 administration did not significantly affect FoxO1 expression.
evidence: This is an observation from the RT-qPCR data in Figure 4E.

claim: FoxO1 and its targets were strongly upregulated upon combined STZ and S961-, or DT-treatment, reflecting a more severe insulin insufficiency.
source: By contrast, FoxO1 and its targets were strongly upregulated upon combined STZ and S961-, or DT-treatment, reflecting a more severe insulin insufficiency (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lack of glucagon signaling efficiently compensates for the consequences of insulin insufficiency only if residual insulin action persists after β-cell loss.
source: Together, these results indicate that lack of glucagon signaling efficiently compensates for the consequences of insulin insufficiency only if residual insulin action persists after β-cell loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data in Figure 4.

claim: In mice injected with 175 mg/kg STZ, anti-GCGR mAb treatment strongly reduced, but did not completely normalize, blood glucose levels.
source: In mice injected with 175 mg/kg STZ, antibody treatment strongly reduced, but did not completely normalize, blood glucose levels (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Animals that had received 225 mg/kg STZ remained severely hyperglycemic (>30 mM) after anti-GCGR mAb administration.
source: By contrast, animals that had received 225 mg/kg STZ remained severely hyperglycemic (>30 mM) after anti-GCGR mAb administration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Residual pancreatic insulin content negatively correlated with the dose of STZ.
source: As expected, residual pancreatic insulin content negatively correlated with the dose of STZ (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by pancreatic insulin measurement data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Beneficial effects of glucagon signaling inhibition were observed only in diabetic mice that had retained a relatively higher pancreatic insulin after STZ-mediated β-cell loss.
source: We thus observed beneficial effects of glucagon signaling inhibition only in diabetic mice that had retained a relatively higher pancreatic insulin after STZ-mediated β-cell loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dose-response data in Figure 5.

claim: The impact of glucagon signaling inhibition on the glycemia of diabetic mice was dependent on very small measurable differences in residual pancreatic insulin, as seen after 175 and 225 mg/kg STZ (respectively 1.79% and 0.45% of the pancreatic insulin content of non-ablated controls).
source: Strikingly, the impact of glucagon signaling inhibition on the glycemia of diabetic mice was dependent on very small measurable differences in residual pancreatic insulin, as seen after 175 and 225 mg/kg STZ (respectively 1.79% and 0.45% of the pancreatic insulin content of non-ablated controls).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative data in Figure 5C.

claim: Regardless the method of β-cell ablation (STZ or DT), the beneficial effects of inhibiting glucagon action, either genetically or pharmacologically, rely upon residual insulin action.
source: Collectively, our findings support the notion that, regardless the method of β-cell ablation (STZ or DT), the beneficial effects of inhibiting glucagon action, either genetically or pharmacologically, rely upon residual insulin action.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental data in the Results section.

claim: One month after DT-mediated β-cell ablation, bihormonal cells were observed in RIP-DTR;Gcgr+/+ and RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice.
source: One month after DT-mediated β-cell ablation, we observed bihormonal cells in RIP-DTR;Gcgr+/+ and RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- animals have α-cell hyperplasia.
source: Because RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- animals have α-cell hyperplasia (Gelling et al., 2003; Longuet et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: The number of bihormonal cells was proportional to the number of α-cells in both RIP-DTR;Gcgr+/+ and RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- groups.
source: and the number of bihormonal cells was proportional to the number of α-cells in both groups (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A significant increase in the absolute number of bihormonal cells was observed in RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice.
source: we observed a significant increase in the absolute number of bihormonal cells in RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice had a higher pancreatic insulin content one month after DT compared to RIP-DTR;Gcgr+/+ mice.
source: Consistent with these observations, they had a higher pancreatic insulin content (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by pancreatic insulin measurement data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There is an increased number of α-cells engaged into reprogramming in mice lacking glucagon signaling.
source: These results indicate that there is an increased number of α-cells engaged into reprogramming in mice lacking glucagon signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bihormonal cell data in Figure 6.

claim: Bihormonal cells appeared in DT-treated adult RIP-DTR mice undergoing anti-GCGR mAb treatment.
source: We also observed the appearance of bihormonal cells in DT-treated adult RIP-DTR mice undergoing anti-GCGR mAb treatment (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: One month after DT injection in Gcgr-/- mice, a significant fraction of insulin-producing cells were also YFP-positive and therefore derived from cells that had previously expressed glucagon.
source: One month after DT injection in Gcgr-/- mice, we observed that a significant fraction of insulin-producing cells were also YFP-positive and therefore derived from cells that had previously expressed glucagon (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Glucagon receptor inhibition decreases hyperglycemia in various animal models of diabetes.
source: Glucagon receptor inhibition decreases hyperglycemia in various animal models of diabetes (Gu et al., 2009; Johnson et al., 1982; Brand et al., 1994; Sloop et al., 2004; Mu et al., 2011; Sorensen et al., 2006)
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: Glucagon receptor inhibition decreases hyperglycemia in patients with type 2 diabetes.
source: as well as in patients with type 2 diabetes (Kelly et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited information from prior clinical studies.

claim: The extent of benefits of glucagon receptor inhibition remains disputed in situations where the β-cell population is nearly completely depleted, as in long-standing type 1 diabetes.
source: The extent of these benefits remains however disputed in situations where the β-cell population is nearly completely depleted, as in long-standing type 1 diabetes (Wang et al., 2012; Meier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature indicating controversy.

claim: Wang et al reported that anti-GCGR mAb treatment was sufficient to normalize glycemia of STZ-treated BALB/c animals.
source: Wang et al reported that anti-GCGR mAb treatment was sufficient to normalize glycemia of STZ-treated BALB/c animals (Wang et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: Steenberg et al did not observe improvements in glucose tolerance after GCGR antagonism or glucagon immunoneutralisation in C57BL/6 mice.
source: whereas Steenberg et al did not observe improvements in glucose tolerance after GCGR antagonism or glucagon immunoneutralisation in C57BL/6 mice (Steenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: Discrepancies between studies may be explained by differences in completeness of β-cell ablation linked to the protocol of injection and/or to strain-dependent sensitivity.
source: These discrepancies may be explained by differences in completeness of β-cell ablation linked to the protocol of injection (single high dose versus multiple low doses) and/or to strain-dependent sensitivity
evidence: This is an inference proposed by the authors to explain conflicting literature.

claim: BALB/c mice are less sensitive to STZ than C57BL/6 animals.
source: it was indeed reported that BALB/c mice are less sensitive to STZ than C57BL/6 animals (Cardinal et al., 1998; Gurley, 2006).
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: A small difference in pancreatic insulin, such as that observed after 175 and 225 mg/kg STZ, can cause a major difference in glycemia in animals lacking glucagon signaling.
source: These results indicate that a small difference in pancreatic insulin, such as that observed after 175 and 225 mg/kg STZ, can cause a major difference in glycemia in animals lacking glucagon signaling, thereby highlighting the importance of residual insulin action and providing a potential explanation for discrepancies between previous studies (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dose-response data in Figure 5.

claim: Lack of glucagon action reduced or normalized glycemia in conditions of less severe insulin deficiency.
source: Although Gcgr-/- mice developed diabetes upon massive β-cell ablation, lack of glucagon action reduced or normalized glycemia in conditions of less severe insulin deficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the STZ dose-response and S961 experiments.

claim: Lack of glucagon signaling counterbalances the effects of insulin insufficiency after STZ or S961 by preventing or limiting the rise in net hepatic glucose output.
source: Our data on hepatic expression of Pepck and Gck, two rate-limiting enzymes of gluconeogenesis and glycolysis, respectively, suggest that lack of glucagon signaling counterbalances the effects of insulin insufficiency after STZ or S961. This would prevent, or limit, the rise in net hepatic glucose output by decreasing gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, and by increasing glycolysis and glycogenesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hepatic gene expression data in Figure 4.

claim: Absence of glucagon action is not sufficient to compensate severe insulin deficiency after DT, as reflected by Gck downregulation and reduced hepatic glycogen content.
source: Absence of glucagon action is however not sufficient to compensate severe insulin deficiency after DT, as reflected by Gck downregulation and reduced hepatic glycogen content, thereby contributing to the elevation of blood glucose.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the hepatic gene expression and glycogen data in Figure 4.

claim: Protection against STZ-mediated hyperglycemia in Gcgr-/- animals also relies on the high levels of circulating glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1).
source: Recent studies have shown that protection against STZ-mediated hyperglycemia also rely on the high levels of circulating glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) in Gcgr-/- animals (Gu et al., 2010; Ali et al., 2011; Jun, 2014; Omar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: High levels of GLP-1 combined with a lack of glucagon action were insufficient to maintain normoglycemia after near-total β-cell loss.
source: Yet, these high levels of GLP-1 combined with a lack of glucagon action were insufficient to maintain normoglycemia after near-total β-cell loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DT experiments in Gcgr-/- mice.

claim: Lack of glucagon signaling does not compromise the ability of α-cells to convert to insulin production after DT-mediated near-total β-cell loss.
source: Finally, we report here that lack of glucagon signaling does not compromise the ability of α-cells to convert to insulin production after DT-mediated near-total β-cell loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lineage tracing data in Figure 6.

claim: YFP-traced α-cells become glucagon/insulin bihormonal cells after DT in RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice and in animals treated with the anti-GCGR antibody.
source: Indeed, YFP-traced α-cells become glucagon/insulin bihormonal cells after DT in RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice and in animals treated with the anti-GCGR antibody (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of α-cells co-expressing insulin after DT is comparable between mice with either intact, reduced or absent glucagon signaling.
source: The proportion of α-cells co-expressing insulin after DT is comparable between mice with either intact, reduced or absent glucagon signaling, indicating that glucagon does not play an essential role in the α-to-β transdifferentiation process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative data in Figure 6B.

claim: Glucagon does not play an essential role in the α-to-β transdifferentiation process.
source: indicating that glucagon does not play an essential role in the α-to-β transdifferentiation process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparable proportions of converting α-cells across genotypes.

claim: Because glucagon signaling inhibition leads to a compensatory α-cell hyperplasia, the absolute number of newly formed insulin-producing cells through α-cell conversion was augmented in RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice.
source: Interestingly, because glucagon signaling inhibition leads to a compensatory α-cell hyperplasia (Furuta et al., 1997; Gelling et al., 2003; Longuet et al., 2013), the absolute number of newly formed insulin-producing cells through α-cell conversion was augmented in RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative data in Figure 6C combined with cited knowledge about α-cell hyperplasia.

claim: δ-to-β conversion was observed in β-cell-ablated RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice.
source: As previously described in adult mice (Chera et al., 2014), we also observed the δ-to-β conversion in β-cell-ablated RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation mentioned but not shown, with citation to prior work.

claim: Although inhibition of glucagon action alone is insufficient to prevent diabetes in conditions of near-total insulin deficiency, it is beneficial when residual insulin action persists.
source: In conclusion, although inhibition of glucagon action alone is insufficient to prevent diabetes in conditions of near-total insulin deficiency, it is beneficial when residual insulin action persists, as in STZ-treated Gcgr-/- animals.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental data.

claim: Combination of glucagon inhibition with insulin therapy may increase the risk of hypoglycemia.
source: Combination of glucagon inhibition with insulin therapy may however increase the risk of hypoglycemia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hypoglycemia observed in insulin pellet experiments.

claim: DT-treated RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice with insulin pellets became hypoglycemic and died likely as a consequence of the constitutive insulin release from the pellets, which could not be compensated by glucagon action.
source: We encountered this problem when using subcutaneous insulin pellets in DT-treated RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice: they became hypoglycemic and died likely as a consequence of the constitutive insulin release from the pellets, which could not be compensated by glucagon action.
evidence: This is an observation from the insulin treatment experiments.

claim: Diabetes therapy through glucagon suppression would be unsafe if exogenous insulin has to be supplemented.
source: Our findings suggest that diabetes therapy through glucagon suppression would be unsafe if exogenous insulin has to be supplemented
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the hypoglycemia risk observed.

claim: Diabetes therapy through glucagon suppression may be beneficial in patients with sufficient residual insulin action.
source: but may be beneficial in patients with sufficient residual insulin action.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: In case of near-total insulin deficiency, transient glucagon receptor blockade could serve as a means to increase the α-cell mass before triggering insulin production in these cells.
source: In case of near-total insulin deficiency, transient glucagon receptor blockade could also serve as a means to increase the α-cell mass before triggering insulin production in these cells, a strategy that might be envisioned as a novel therapy to treat diabetes.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for future therapy based on the α-cell conversion findings.

claim: RIP-DTR mice lead to >99% β-cell loss after DT injection.
source: For this purpose, we crossed Gcgr-/- mutant animals (Gelling et al., 2003) with RIP-DTR mice, in which diphtheria toxin (DT) injection triggers the near-total (>99% ) β-cell loss (Thorel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited information about the RIP-DTR model.

claim: Survival of DT-treated RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice was significantly different from RIP-DTR;Gcgr+/- mice (p=0.044).
source: Survival analysis of DT-treated animals (Gcgr+/- versus Gcgr-/-): p=0.044; Log-rank test.
evidence: This is a statistical result from survival analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice remained markedly hyperglucagonemic after STZ- or DT-mediated β-cell loss.
source: RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- animals remained markedly hyperglucagonemic after STZ- or DT-mediated β-cell loss and α-cell mass was not affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by plasma glucagon measurement data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: α-cell mass was not affected after STZ- or DT-mediated β-cell loss in RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- mice.
source: RIP-DTR;Gcgr-/- animals remained markedly hyperglucagonemic after STZ- or DT-mediated β-cell loss and α-cell mass was not affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by α-cell mass measurement data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: S961 administration in vivo closely recapitulates the phenotype of mice with liver-specific insulin receptor deletion.
source: In vivo, S961 administration induces hyperglycemia in wild type animals and closely recapitulates the phenotype of mice with liver-specific insulin receptor deletion (Yi et al., 2013; Michael et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited information about the S961 drug.

claim: Liver is a relevant organ to assess the impact of insulin and glucagon deficiency because re-expression of the glucagon receptor in the liver of STZ-treated Gcgr-/- mice is sufficient to trigger hyperglycemia.
source: Liver is a relevant organ to assess the impact of insulin and glucagon deficiency because re-expression of the glucagon receptor in the liver of STZ-treated Gcgr-/- mice, and conditional inactivation of the insulin receptor in hepatocytes are both sufficient to trigger hyperglycemia (Lee et al., 2012; Michael et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: Conditional inactivation of the insulin receptor in hepatocytes is sufficient to trigger hyperglycemia.
source: Liver is a relevant organ to assess the impact of insulin and glucagon deficiency because re-expression of the glucagon receptor in the liver of STZ-treated Gcgr-/- mice, and conditional inactivation of the insulin receptor in hepatocytes are both sufficient to trigger hyperglycemia (Lee et al., 2012; Michael et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: Gonadal adipose tissue was markedly depleted in experimental conditions leading to hyperglycemia (in Gcgr-/- mice after STZ+S961 and DT; in Gcgr+/- mice after STZ and DT).
source: In addition, gonadal adipose tissue was markedly depleted in experimental conditions leading to hyperglycemia (in Gcgr-/- mice after STZ+S691 and DT; in Gcgr+/- mice after STZ and DT; not shown).
evidence: This is an observation mentioned but not shown in figures.

claim: Protection against STZ-mediated hyperglycemia in Gcgr-/- animals relies on the high levels of circulating GLP-1.
source: Recent studies have shown that protection against STZ-mediated hyperglycemia also rely on the high levels of circulating glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) in Gcgr-/- animals (Gu et al., 2010; Ali et al., 2011; Jun, 2014; Omar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: Pups born from Gcgr-/- mothers die perinatally.
source: As pups born from Gcgr-/- mothers die perinatally (Vuguin et al., 2006), Gcgr+/- females were used for breeding.
evidence: This is cited information from prior literature.

claim: Blood glucose was measured from tail blood using a handheld glucometer with a detection range of 0.6 to 33.3 mM.
source: Blood glucose was measured from tail blood using a handheld glucometer (detection range: 0.6 to 33.3 mM, values exceeding 33.3 mM were artificially set to 34 mM).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about glucose measurement.

claim: For β-cell ablation in RIP-DTR mice, DT was injected i.p. in 3 injections of 125 ng each, at days 0, 3, and 4.
source: For β-cell ablation in RIP-DTR mice, DT (D0564, Sigma, St. Louis, MO) was injected i.p. in 3 injections of 125 ng each, at days 0, 3, and 4.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about DT administration.
